title: Gold coins on the ground
hookLine: Anathapindika covers Prince Jeta's grove with gold coins to buy it for the monks (Vinaya, Cullavagga 6)

cards: A merchant from Savatthi arrives in Rajagaha on business and finds his brother-in-law's house in an uproar: cooking for a crowd, servants rushing about. Is there a wedding? Has the king been invited?
No, says the brother-in-law. The Buddha and his monks are coming for a meal tomorrow. The merchant stops at that word, Buddha.
He meets the teacher, hears him, and asks him to spend the rainy season in his own city, with the monks. The awakened, the Buddha answers, delight in quiet places. Understood, says the merchant.
The texts call him Anathapindika. Today, the price he paid for a quiet place.

teach.b: First, the place. Back home, Anathapindika looks for land for the monks: not too far from town, not too near, easy to reach, quiet at night. He finds a grove belonging to Prince Jeta, and asks to buy it.
The prince doesn't want to sell: not even if you covered it in gold coins. Then it's sold, says Anathapindika. The prince protests that he named no such deal.

The Vinaya says they took it to the officials who settled such matters, and the officials ruled that a price had been named. Third, the gold. Anathapindika has gold brought out in carts and laid across the ground.

teach.h: CARTS OF COINS, ONE BARE PATCH.
teach.b: One small patch near the gateway is still bare, and he sends for more. That's when the prince changes his mind. A man wouldn't spend like this, he thinks, unless the thing were truly worth it.
He asks to give that last patch himself, and builds a gateway on it. So the place carries two names: Jeta's grove, Anathapindika's park. Fourth, the gift.
Anathapindika builds dwellings, halls, storerooms and wells.

teach.h: FOR THE SANGHA OF FOUR DIRECTIONS.
teach.b: When he asks how to give it, the Buddha tells him: to the sangha of the four directions, those present and those still to come.

Sutta after sutta opens with that place in its first line: the Blessed One was staying at Savatthi, in Jeta's grove, Anathapindika's park. Discourse after discourse, framed by one man's gold and one prince's gateway.

how: In Buddhist communities lay people support monasteries with gifts of land, buildings, food and robes; giving a dwelling to the sangha is a traditional act of merit, and the story of Jeta's grove is retold when such gifts are made.

o: a forest where hermits lived alone
Jeta's grove, a park given to the monks
a king's hunting ground near Rajagaha

games.q: buying Jeta's grove: tap the pairs.
p: not even if you covered it in gold
the prince's own gift: a gateway

s: Prince Jeta was eager to sell his grove
he named an impossible price to say no, and was held to it.
the prince ended up giving part of the ground himself
he asked to give the last bare patch, and built a gateway on it.
Anathapindika gave the grove to the Buddha alone
the Buddha told him to give it to the sangha of the four directions, present and to come.

games.q: you're Anathapindika. Prince Jeta says he wouldn't sell his grove even if you covered it in gold coins. what do you do?
o: walk away and look for other land.
take him at his word and bring the gold.
offer double what the land is worth.
games.why: he says, then it's sold. the officials agree a price was named, and the carts of gold roll in until only one patch by the gate is left bare.

practice: Think of one thing you could give, some time, a meal, your full attention, a tool you never use, and watch for the small pull to keep a patch bare, to give a little less than you first meant.
You don't have to fight it; just see it, the way Anathapindika saw the bare ground by the gate.

wordCard.voice: Jetavana. Jeta's grove, which Anathapindika covered in gold to buy for the monks, with the prince giving the last patch himself. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali Jetavana: Jeta's grove, the park at Savatthi that Anathapindika bought for the monks.

carryVoice: Your line: covered in gold. Even the prince who wouldn't sell ended up giving. Day seven hundred sixty-seven, done.
